trans-unit.source: Triage trackers reported by the SimpleCMP CMS bridge and manage the registered service catalog. Approve recognised detections, curate new services for unknown trackers, and promote registry entries to the visitor banner.

Each row captures the resolved banner configuration (services, theme, translation overrides, Site Settings) at the moment of an editor save. Identical-content re-saves dedupe by sha256 — only material changes create new rows. Use these snapshots to prove the exact banner state shown to visitors at any point in time.
Edits to the site configuration (`config/sites/<id>/settings.yaml`) don't auto-snapshot. After such an edit, run:
No snapshots yet for this site. Edit a service / theme / translation override, or run the CLI command above.

No textual difference between the snapshots (rare; possible if pretty-printing collapsed cosmetic changes).
This is the first snapshot for this site — nothing to diff against.

Every accept / decline / save click logged by visitors while this snapshot was the active banner configuration. The visitor identifier is pseudonymized (HMAC-SHA256 of the visitor's UUID with the bridge secret) so the raw UUID never lands in the database. Identical decisions from the same visitor deduplicate via a UNIQUE constraint.
No visitor decisions have been logged against this snapshot version yet.
Showing the %d most recent of %d decisions. Older entries are accessible via direct DB query (CSV export coming in Phase 3).

Admin-mediated lookup of a visitor's consent history. The visitor supplies their raw UUID (from their browser); the server pseudonymizes it with the bridge secret and returns every decision row plus the snapshots those decisions were made against. The raw UUID is never persisted server-side.
Where does the visitor find their UUID?

Each snapshot is the exact banner configuration that was active when the visitor confirmed. Expand to inspect the canonical content.

Counts the runtime classifier's queries to the upstream registry — independent of this panel's freshness probe. Stays at 0 when the bundled library is in sync with upstream: in that state, upstream calls are skipped because the bundled tier already saw the same data.

Park this detection — it will stop showing in the actionable list and will not reappear even if visitors keep triggering it. Reversible from the Dismissed view.

Allow this host's stylesheets to load normally (stops blocking its CSS). Scoped to stylesheets — scripts and iframes from the same host stay blocked. Prefer self-hosting for fonts (e.g. Google Fonts) where you can.

Allowing reloads this host's CSS without consent. The durable fix is self-hosting the stylesheet (e.g. download the Google Font and serve it from your own domain) — then no third-party request is made at all.
Third-party stylesheets aren't being blocked yet

Universal blocking is on for this site, but third-party CSS (e.g. Google Fonts at fonts.googleapis.com) still loads before consent — which sends the visitor's IP to the third party. Enabling stylesheet blocking moves it behind consent. It's best-effort: the browser's preload scanner can fetch a stylesheet before the rewriter intervenes, and @import inside a stylesheet escapes entirely.
The durable fix is self-hosting — serve fonts and CSS from your own domain so no third-party request happens at all.
Move this detection back into the actionable list.

The HMAC secret used to authenticate visitor reports is normally generated when you first open this module. The automatic generation didn't succeed — typically because `config/system/settings.php` isn't writable by PHP. Retry with the button below, or run `vendor/bin/typo3 simplecmp:generate-bridge-secret` from a shell and follow its instructions.
Visitor browsers can send tracker reports to this list.
Generate a fresh HMAC secret. Visitor pages loaded before rotation will get one 401 cycle until they re-issue a nonce on next page render.
Rotate the bridge HMAC secret? Visitor pages currently loaded will need one 401 cycle to re-issue their nonce on next render. Continue?
Look up every currently-unknown cookie / host in the upstream library and store the matches in the local cache. Unknown rows that match upstream will surface as Erkannt on the next list render.

Walks the site's sitemap inside your browser. Each page loads in a hidden frame; the detection chain records cookies and external services as it would for any visitor. You can leave this tab running and come back when it's done.

Provision Matomo, Google Analytics, Google Tag Manager, Meta Pixel, or Microsoft UET without writing code. Each tracker registered here gets a Service-DB row, a CSP origin whitelist, and (where applicable) a consent-gated loader script — all automatic.
No BE-managed trackers yet. Click "Add" to set one up.
%d tracker(s) defined in the site configuration are awaiting editor adoption — manage them in the Settings tab.
No sites configured. Add a site under Sites & Settings first.
Base URL of the install, with trailing slash (https://matomo.example.com/)
Override for setups with two Matomo instances. Default: "matomo".
Default ON (DACH compliance). Disable only with a documented reason.
Pick exactly one. The two modes are mutually exclusive — combining them is the ADR-0016 anti-pattern (it silently suppresses GA4 even after consent).
gtag/js is not loaded until the visitor accepts. No third-party traffic pre-consent. The legally tightest choice in Germany / Austria / Switzerland.

gtag/js loads pre-consent and sends cookieless pings. The CMP emits gtag('consent','update',…) on accept. Better measurement; the cookieless ping is still a Google network call several DACH/EU regulators contest.
Pick exactly one. GTM signal-gate only bites for tags that opt into Consent Mode v2 inside the GTM console (Built-in Consent Settings); tags without that config will still fire pre-consent.
gtm.js is not loaded until the visitor accepts. No tags inside the container can fire pre-consent. The legally tightest choice in Germany / Austria / Switzerland.

gtm.js loads pre-consent so the container can fire tags with cookieless pings or in basic mode. The CMP emits gtag('consent','update',…) on accept. Verify every tag inside the container has its Consent Settings configured — otherwise tags WILL fire unrestricted.

15–16 digit Meta Pixel ID from Events Manager. Meta Pixel is signal-only — your existing pixel template keeps loading fbevents.js; SimpleCMP only dispatches fbq('consent', …) on accept / withdraw. Hard pre-consent suppression for Meta is handled by Universal Blocking (load-gating).
Override for setups with two Meta pixels on one site. Default: "meta-pixel".
7–10 digit UET Tag ID from Microsoft Advertising → Tools → UET Tag. Drives both bat.js initialization and the Service-DB description.
Pick exactly one. Microsoft mandated the Consent Mode signal as of May 2025 — running UET without it risks the account being flagged as non-compliant in advertising audits.
bat.js is not loaded until the visitor accepts. The window.uetq queue is still pre-created and any customer-pushed events queue safely until accept. No third-party traffic pre-consent.

bat.js loads pre-consent; the CMP emits uetq.push('consent', 'default'/'update', {ad_storage}) so Microsoft honours the visitor's decision. Choose this when you need Microsoft's "Consent Mode signal" account status to flip compliant.
Override for setups with two UET tags on one site. Default: "microsoft-uet".
Using more than 2 trackers? Consider a Tag Manager.

Each extra tracker multiplies CSP entries, Service-DB rows, and editor friction. A Tag Manager (Matomo TM for privacy-first, Google TM for marketing-driven sites) reduces all of that to a single SimpleCMP service — and lets marketing add or swap tags without TYPO3 deployments. Server-side TM goes further: first-party cookies, no third-party DNS, ITP-resilient.
